summary:
Sky Time Machine is an interactive web platform for exploring how the sky changes over time, using real observations from NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope. Users search any object or coordinate and see every archived SPHEREx exposure covering that position. They can compare two observation dates through a blink comparator, a difference image and uncertainty maps, and investigate ranked change candidates through shareable links.

SPHEREx surveys the whole sky repeatedly, but its data is hard to compare across time because each part of its detector sees a different wavelength. Our pipeline calculates the wavelength of every pixel and compares only matching observations. It also aligns the images, corrects for blur differences using NASA’s own PSF models, removes zodiacal light, and flags artifacts. Every candidate comes with measured uncertainties, quality checks, a plain-language explanation and full data provenance. An AI assistant answers questions grounded only in these stored measurements.

This makes time-domain astronomy accessible to students, citizen scientists and researchers without specialist software. It stays scientifically honest: nothing is simulated, and nothing is presented as a discovery without evidence.
details:
Sky Time Machine is “Google Maps for the sky with a time slider,” built on real data from NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope.

Explore: search any object (e.g. “M31”) or coordinates on an interactive sky map showing SPHEREx coverage, known objects and constellations.

Timeline: see every real SPHEREx observation of that spot, with dates, coverage gaps and the wavelength each observation recorded there.

Compare: pick two dates and view them in a blink comparator (flickering between them), side by side, or as a difference image with uncertainty and quality masks.

Discoveries: detected changes are ranked, graded A/B/R, explained in plain language, and cross-matched against the SIMBAD and Gaia catalogues. Each one has a permanent shareable link.

Spectra and light curves: measure an object’s brightness across SPHEREx’s 102 wavelength channels and over time.

Investigations and watchlists: save findings into reports, and get notified when NASA releases new data for a region.

Sky Intelligence: an AI assistant that answers questions using only stored measurements, and always separates measurement from interpretation.

Behind the scenes: the backend queries NASA’s IRSA archive, downloads only the bytes it needs, validates each FITS file, and aligns the two images onto one sky grid. It keeps only pixels seen at the same wavelength, matches the blur between images using NASA’s PSF models, removes zodiacal light, and subtracts the images. It then detects changes at 5σ or more, rejects artifacts and ranks the results. Every step is recorded so results can be reproduced.

Benefits

Accessible: professional time-domain analysis in a browser, with no specialist software.

Trustworthy: real NASA data only, uncertainties on every number, original data clearly separated from processed products, and full provenance.

Efficient: reads small byte ranges instead of whole 65 MB files, and caches results.

Shareable: every view and candidate has a permanent link, and reports can be exported.

Extensible: adding another telescope only needs a new data adapter.

Intended impact

Help students, educators and citizen scientists explore real space-telescope data and learn how astronomers find changes in the sky.

Give researchers a fast way to screen SPHEREx data for variable sources, transients and moving objects worth following up.

Model scientific honesty in AI tools: the system never claims a discovery without evidence.

Tools, languages and software

Area Tools

Languages Python, TypeScript, SQL

Backend FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLAlchemy, Alembic, SQLite

Science Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, reproject, photutils

Frontend Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Aladin Lite (sky map)

Data APIs NASA/IPAC IRSA (SIA, IBE cutouts, HiPS tiles, AWS mirror), CDS Sesame, SIMBAD, Gaia DR3

AI Anthropic Claude API (optional; a rule-based mode works without it)

Quality pytest, Vitest, ruff, mypy, ESLint, GitHub Actions CI

Dev Git, GitHub, Claude Code (AI-assisted development)

Hardware A standard laptop (macOS); no GPU or special hardware needed

How it’s creative

Wavelength-aware comparison. SPHEREx sees a different colour at each spot on its detector, so naive “before vs after” comparisons are misleading. We compute every pixel’s wavelength and compare like with like. This is the project’s core insight.

Cross-convolution blur matching. We blur each image with the other’s blur pattern, so both end up identical without amplifying noise. We checked the orientation of NASA’s PSF models by fitting real stars.

Blink comparator: a 100-year-old astronomer’s technique (used to find Pluto) rebuilt for the web.

Honest AI: the assistant cites stored records and labels hypotheses, instead of making confident claims.

Original vs derived labels on every image, so users always know what is NASA’s data and what is our processing.

Factors the team considered

Scientific integrity: no fabricated data; synthetic data only in tests, labelled as such; every candidate unverified until reviewed.

Accuracy: uncertainty propagation, artifact checks, injection-recovery tests on real data, and documented limitations.

Reproducibility: deterministic comparison IDs, software versions and full provenance.

Usability and accessibility: keyboard controls, mobile layout, plain-language explanations.

Performance: byte-range reads, caching, background jobs.

Reliability: retries for NASA server outages, and graceful fallbacks when there’s no AI key or no PSF model.

Community safety: moderation, an audit log, and votes that can never “confirm” a discovery.

Openness: public GitHub repository, free public APIs, open-source libraries.
